papers.title_in_file: Quantum-Assisted Vehicle Routing: Realizing QAOA-based Approach on Gate-Based Quantum Computer
papers.version_note: arXiv:2505.01614v3, 27 Jan 2026. The text layer printed math symbols as unreadable glyphs; quotes avoid them.
papers.what_it_is: A link-based QAOA formulation of the vehicle routing problem run on IBM hardware, with a solved 3-node case and failed or poor 4 and 5 node cases.

existing.note: The paper says later (Section 4.5) that with coefficient normalization applied, QAOA for the 4-node problem recovered the correct solution among the most frequently sampled bitstrings. The paper does not say whether the 2 hour infeasible run used normalization.
existing.value: The authors report that a 4 node problem took over 2 hours to run on the quantum computer and generated an infeasible solution, with the top 10 most sampled states all infeasible. The authors also report that with normalization applied, QAOA for the 4-node problem was able to recover the correct solution among the most frequently sampled bitstrings.
quotes: This problem took over 2 hours to run on the quantum computer and generated an infeasible solution.
In fact, the top 10 most sampled states were all infeasible.
With normalization applied, QAOA for the 4-node problem was able to recover the correct solution among the most frequently sampled bitstrings.

existing.certainty_reason: Abstract, p.1 and Section 4.6, p.19: the authors state the limit themselves.

assertions.value: The authors state that a randomly instantiated VRP with 3 nodes and 2 vehicles was formulated with the link based formulation, and that the QAOA was implemented on the 127 qubit IBM-Rensselaer quantum computer with depth 2.
quotes: A randomly instantiated VRP with 3 nodes and 2 vehicles was formulated using the link based formulation
implemented on the 127 qubit IBM-Rensselaer quantum computer
depth of 2
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.1 and 4.2 state the experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors report that the most likely bit-string sampled was 111010, and that it has been verified with a classical solver as the optimum solution.
quotes: the most likely bit-string is 111010
It has been verified with a classical solver that this is the optimum solution.

assertions.value: The authors report that suboptimal solutions were also sampled with non-negligible frequencies, which they attribute to noise in the quantum hardware, low depth p, and limitations of the standard QAOA.
quotes: However, the probability distribution also shows that suboptimal solutions were sampled with non-negligible frequencies
assertions.reader_inference: The attribution to noise, low depth and standard QAOA is the authors' suggestion (a behavior that could be attributed), not a tested cause.

assertions.value: The authors report that the optimization process took around 14 minutes and that the final circuit was executed for 10,000 shots, taking about 15 seconds of wall clock time.
quotes: the optimization process took around 14 minutes
the circuit executed again for 10,000 shots
which take about 15

assertions.value: The authors report that a 4 node problem with depth of 2 generates a 14 qubit circuit.
quotes: a 4 node problem with depth of 2 generates a 14 qubit circuit

assertions.value: The authors report that a 5 node problem with depth 2 transpiled into a 30 qubit circuit of about 30,000 basic gates.
quotes: a 5 node problem with depth 2 transpiled into a 30 qubit circuit of about 30,000 basic gates

assertions.value: The authors report that using leave-one-out cross-validation on four problem sizes, a quadratic fit exhibits lower prediction error than an exponential one, consistent with quadratic scaling of two-qubit gate depth over the tested range.
quotes: Using leave-one-out cross-validation on four problem sizes, a quadratic fit exhibits lower prediction error than an exponential one
assertions.reader_inference: Four problem sizes is a small sample; the fit does not show quadratic scaling beyond the tested range.

assertions.value: The authors state that the subtour elimination constraints increase exponentially with the number of nodes, since there is one constraint for every subset of nodes, giving an exponentially increasing number of terms in the QUBO and Ising Hamiltonian.
quotes: since there is one constraint for every subset of nodes
As a result, there ends up being an exponentially increasing number of terms in the QUBO and, therefore, the Ising Hamiltonian.
assertions.certainty_reason: Limit stated by the authors; no proof given.

assertions.value: The authors report that the edge-based formulation requires a lower two-qubit gate depth across all cases than the time-expanded and route-order formulations, which they judge impractical on current hardware because of their substantially larger QUBO sizes.
quotes: The edge-based formulation requires a lower two-qubit gate depth across all cases.
their substantially larger QUBO sizes and resulting two-qubit gate depths render them impractical on current quantum hardware

assertions.value: The authors report that choosing either substantially higher or lower penalty values did not improve performance, and that setting the penalty coefficient to twice the sum of edge weights was found to consistently yield the most reliable results.
quotes: Choosing either substantially higher or lower penalty values did not improve performance.
setting the penalty coefficient to twice the sum of edge weights was found to consistently yield the most reliable results
assertions.reader_inference: The grid of penalty values tested is shown only in Figure 11 (4 node problem).

assertions.value: The authors report that normalizing the Pauli coefficients so that all magnitudes were bounded by one improved performance, particularly for larger problem instances with 4 and 5 nodes, and that without normalization the algorithm failed to consistently identify the optimal route in the high probability region of the output distribution.
quotes: normalization improved performance, particularly for larger problem instances with 4 and 5 nodes
Without normalization, however, the algorithm failed to consistently identify the optimal route in the high probability region of the output distribution.
This observation was consistent across multiple randomly generated 4 and 5 node instances.

assertions.value: The authors report that without normalization, feasibility of the top 1000 most frequently sampled bitstrings remains low across all penalty values, and that with normalization the feasibility ratio peaks at over 2%, around multipliers of 1.5-2.0.
quotes: Without normalization, feasibility remains low across all penalty values, showing only small fluctuations.
where the feasibility ratio peaks at over 2%
feasibility ratio of the top 1000 most frequently sampled bitstrings
particularly around multipliers of 1.5–2.0
assertions.reader_inference: A peak feasibility ratio of about 2% means that at most about 2 in 100 of the top sampled bitstrings were feasible on the 4 node problem; the authors call this an improvement.

assertions.value: The authors state that error suppression was applied to the circuit in the form of dynamic decoupling, and that Pauli twirling was also used in the experiments.
quotes: Error suppression was applied to the circuit in the form of dynamic decoupling
and was also used in the experiments.

assertions.value: The authors state that the IBM-Rensselaer quantum computer has 127 qubits, which puts a limit on the size of any problem that can be executed on it.
quotes: The IBM-Rensselaer quantum computer has 127 qubits, which puts a limit on the size of any problem that can be executed on it.

assertions.value: The authors state that the observed exponential growth in circuit complexity caused by the problem mapping leads to significant decoherence and noise accumulation, reducing solution accuracy.
quotes: The observed exponential growth in circuit complexity caused by the problem mapping leads to significant decoherence and noise accumulation, reducing solution accuracy.

assertions.value: The authors state that, with unbalanced penalization, the penalty coefficients would have to be optimized classically for every problem beforehand.
quotes: Moreover, the penalty coefficients would have to be optimized classically for every problem beforehand.

assertions.value: The authors state that the optimization landscape of QAOA becomes increasingly complex as the number of qubits grows, leading to an exponential increase in the number of function evaluations required for parameter tuning.
quotes: leading to an exponential increase in the number of function evaluations required for parameter tuning

assertions.value: The authors conclude that for larger instances the rapid growth in circuit depth, specifically two-qubit gate depth, poses a significant practical challenge due to the limitations of noisy quantum processors.
quotes: the rapid growth in circuit depth, specifically two-qubit gate depth, poses a significant practical challenge due to the limitations of noisy quantum processors

assertions.value: The authors state that, rather than proposing a new algorithmic variant, they systematically expose the practical bottlenecks that arise when mapping constrained routing problems onto real quantum processors.
quotes: Rather than proposing a new algorithmic variant, we systematically expose the practical bottlenecks that arise when mapping constrained routing problems onto real quantum processors.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5 states the paper's own scope.
